citations.title: Anticipatory Action for climate shocks | World Food Programme
excerpts: One of WFP's flagship programmes to manage climate-related risks is its Anticipatory Action (AA) for climate shocks programme, previously known as Forecast Based Financing (FbF). **The AA programme enables the implementation and financing of actions before an extreme weather event has occurred.** These anticipatory actions aim to prevent and mitigate – to the extent possible – the effects of extreme weather on the food security and nutrition of highly vulnerable people.

**Launched in 2015, WFP’s AA portfolio now includes 44 countries in Asia and the Pacific, Africa, and Latin America and the Caribbean.** WFP, together with national and local government partners, is supporting the development of early-warning systems and anticipatory actions for critical natural hazards such as droughts, floods and cyclones.

44 countries where WFP is developing Anticipatory Action programmes alongside governments and other key humanitarian partners, in Africa, Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean More than 6.2 million people protected with anticipatory action in 2024
WFP is scaling up its AA programme and can currently reach 350,000 people five days before a forecasted flood, using mobile money and early warning messaging.

Bangladesh WFP has successfully implemented Anticipatory Action, working with the national government and humanitarian partners [including the Red Crescent Movement.](https://docs.wfp.org/api/documents/WFP-0000135358/download/) AA was implemented before severe monsoon floods that devastated vulnerable communities in the country's northeast in 2020.

AA in Bangladesh has [shown a positive impact](https://www.wfp.org/publications/acting-flood-protect-most-vulnerable-independent-review-wfps-anticipatory-cash) on families' food security; 36 percent fewer people went a day without eating throughout the floods, when they received assistance.

excerpts: Credit shortages, lack of insurance, inadequate training, and poorly functioning in- put and output markets prevent the poorest farmers from accessing these innovations or effectively managing associated risks.

Poor and smallholder farmers typically experience multiple interre- lated constraints that impedes their adoption of agricultural technologies. They lack access to affordable credit and savings, have few risk-management options, receive inadequate training or information on new practices, and face high transaction costs and weak input and output markets. Even when subsidies or pilot programs reduce upfront costs, residual expenses, remaining risks and uncertainty about returns often keep innovations out of reach. In practice, technology uptake requires functioning credit systems, effective extension services and reliable market access; without these foundations, any gains tend to be modest or short-lived, particularly for the poorest households (De Janvry and Sadoulet 2002, Duflo et al. 2008, Porteous 2020).

Climate change significantly exacerbates these existing barriers to technology adoption. Smallholder farmers, especially those already facing limited resources and market access, are disproportionately vulnerable to increasingly frequent and severe climate shocks such as droughts, floods, and temperature extremes. Low productivity often compels them to expand cultivation onto marginal lands, accelerating defor- estation, soil degradation, and water stress. Under such conditions, poor households resort to costly coping mechanisms like reducing food intake or depleting savings, fur- ther undermining their ability to invest in yield-enhancing inputs or services (FAO, 2022). Historical limitations in adopting traditional agricultural technologies have already left these farmers highly susceptible to environmental stressors, and climate change is likely to intensify these vulnerabilities.

Credit and financial constraints are well-documented barriers to the adoption of modern agricultural technologies among smallholder farmers in developing countries, with direct implications for productivity and welfare (Bridle et al., 2020; Suri and Udry, 2022). These constraints operate in two main ways. First, the high costs of inputs such as high-yield seeds, fertilizers, and mechanization often exceed the means of resource-poor farmers who have limited or no savings. Second, even when these technologies offer higher long-term returns, limited access to credit discourages their adoption because of the perceived risk (Diagne et al., 2000; Guirkinger and Boucher, 2008; Dercon and Christiaensen, 2011). While formal financial services have the potential to ease capital constraints, ac- cess remains limited for many farmers due to a range of structural and institutional barriers. These include mismatches between loan repayment schedules and agri- cultural cycles (Burke et al., 2017), stringent collateral requirements (Feder et al., 1988), high perceived risk among lenders (Stiglitz and Weiss, 1981), low levels of financial literacy (Su et al., 2024), high transaction costs (Balana et al., 2022), gen- der disparities in financial access (Adegbite and Machethe, 2020), and limited rural banking infrastructure (Ali et al., 2014a). These risks often constrain their willingness and ability to invest in productivity-enhancing tech- nologies. Informal coping mechanisms such as asset sales, community support, and precautionary savings offer partial protection but are generally inadequate for manag- ing widespread shocks like droughts, floods, or sharp market declines. (2013) highlights demand-side challenges such as lack of trust, limited liquidity, and poor understand- ing of insurance products. Insurance uptake is also affected by the interaction be- tween technology risk and household vulnerability. High-yield varieties often carry higher variance in outcomes, making them riskier for farmers already facing unstable conditions (Gatti et al., 2023). Insecure land tenure and uncertainty about future returns further discourage long-term investments (Fafchamps, 2009; Suri and Udry, 2022). Low adoption of agricultural insurance stems not only from demand-side con- straints but also from fundamental design and pricing challenges. Traditional indemnity- based insurance, which bases payouts on verified on-farm losses, is often too costly 6 and impractical to administer in remote rural areas. To address this, index insurance has emerged as a key innovation. It links payouts to objectively measurable indica- tors such as rainfall, temperature, or vegetation indices, which reduces verification costs and administrative burdens. This makes it more attractive for insurers and governments aiming to expand coverage efficiently (Ceballos et al., 2025). However, index insurance presents its own limitations. Many products are de- signed to insure frequent, localized risks such as seasonal droughts or pest outbreaks. Because these events occur often, maintaining actuarial soundness requires high pre- miums, which are typically unaffordable without substantial public subsidies (Cebal- los et al., 2025). This creates fiscal challenges, particularly in settings with limited public budgets. In these cases, preventive strategies such as early warning systems, improved agronomic practices, or drought-tolerant seed varieties may be more cost- effective than insurance (Clarke and Dercon, 2016). In addition, structural issues such as basis risk—the mismatch between actual losses and index-triggered pay- outs—can reduce trust and deter uptake. Developing accurate indices that reflect farm-level realities is inherently difficult due to variation in crop types, local grow- ing conditions, and farming practices. These constraints help explain why adoption remains limited, even when products are subsidized and designed to be accessible.

Many farmers are unaware of improved inputs or do not know how to apply them effectively, leading to contin- ued reliance on traditional, lower-yielding practices (Suri and Udry, 2022). Public- sector extension systems have historically attempted to address this gap (Jayne et al., 2023), but in many low- and middle-income countries they face persistent challenges. In sub-Saharan Africa, for example, farmer-to-extension worker ratios often exceed 1,000 to 1, limiting the reach and effectiveness of these programs (Fabregas et al., 2019). Access to both input and output markets plays a critical role in determining small- holder farmers’ productivity and welfare. Farmers frequently encounter barriers such as high transaction costs, weak infrastructure, and fragmented supply chains, which reduce their access to quality inputs and limit participation in profitable output markets. These challenges weaken incentives to adopt productivity-enhancing tech- 9 nologies, as higher yields may not lead to increased incomes (Barrett et al., 2010; Bridle et al., 2020). Poor contract enforcement, limited price differentiation for higher-quality produce, and the dominance of intermediaries further constrain mar- ket participation, especially for smallholders (Miguel, 2024). On the input side, farmers often face limited availability of quality seeds, fertiliz- ers, and credit, as well as information asymmetries that reduce the efficiency of input use. Saenger et al. (2014) find that greater transparency around product quality can improve input use, especially when price premiums for higher-quality output exist. Nuru has three components to its artificial intelligence: 1) human expert level crop disease diagnostics using computer vision; 2) above human capabilities in anomaly detection and forecasting based on ground and satellite derived data; and 3) human language comprehension and automated responses to questions posed by farmers.
One farmer invented a novel use for the tool by using it to diagnose healthy cassava crops.
Nuru was, on average, twice as accurate as the extension workers she was tested against.

Nuru AI has been downloaded by users from all continents and widely used in Africa and South East Asia by the end of June 2018.

excerpts: In the evaluation sample, we randomly assigned farmers to either a treatment group, which received access to Ama Krushi, or a control group, which did not. ³ To minimize the spillover of information between the treatment and control farmers that might affect the impact estimates, we capped the proportion of farmers receiving access to Ama Krushi at 15% of farming households in each panchayat.

We collected self-reported data via two rounds of follow-up surveys to measure Ama Krushi’s impact on farmer outcomes, including agricultural knowledge, practice adoption, rice yield, crop loss, and agricultural profits.
This evaluation focused on rice advisory during the 2021 and 2022 “Kharif” seasons (the main agricultural season in India).
The final study sample included 13,675 farmers across 902 villages in 18 blocks of the five districts.
The key findings we discuss in this blog are primarily based on the survey data collected from 5,204 farmers.
These districts were not randomly selected but covered multiple agroclimatic zones. .

**Two-way voice-based platform:** Farmers receive weekly recorded messages with timely agricultural advice on their mobile phones. They can also call a hotline to access agricultural advice on demand, or record questions. Local agronomists respond to these questions with recorded audio messages, which are sent back to farmers within 48 hours.
The average yield was 1.7% higher per season, and the average harvest was 4.1% higher per season over the two Kharif seasons.
In comparison, treatment farmers with access to Ama Krushi had a 10% lower incidence of severe crop loss.

This includes a 9.4% increase in rice harvest in areas hit by excess rainfall in Year 1, a similarly large but statistically insignificant increase in rice harvest in areas hit by inadequate rainfall in Year 2, and a 21% reduction in severe crop loss in those areas hit by inadequate rainfall.
_Notes: Unless noted otherwise, the results we highlight here are statistically significant at 10% after adjusting for multiple hypothesis tests (MHT).
Our self-reported profit measures have very large variances, meaning that our analysis leaves some uncertainty about whether increased profits were just caused by random chance.
We did not collect sufficiently granular data on the timing of specific agricultural practices to pin down the impact mechanisms.
Importantly, Ama Krushi does not protect farmers against every weather-related shock.

excerpts: The Prime Minister Street Vendor's AtmaNirbhar Nidhi (PM SVANidhi) scheme, an initiative under the aegis of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA), has achieved a momentous milestone by extending its support to more than 50 lakh street vendors across the nation.
PM SVANidhi is a pioneering initiative by the Government of India aimed at integrating street vendors into the formal economic system and facilitating access to formal channels of credit.

The PM Street Vendor's AtmaNirbharNidhi (PM SVANidhi) Scheme, launched on June 1, 2020, is a micro credit scheme for urban street vendors that aims to provide collateral-free working capital loans up to ₹50,000.
This collective endeavor resulted in disbursement of a remarkable 65.75 lakh loans, benefiting over 50 lakh street vendors, with a total value exceeding ₹ 8600 crore.
Under the scheme regular repayments are incentivized with a 7% interest subsidy and digital transactions are rewarded with cashback up to ₹1,200 per year.
These collaborations have resulted in over 113.2 Crore digital transactions worth ₹1,33,003 Crores, with ₹58.2 Crore in cashback disbursed to beneficiaries.
The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs remains steadfast in its commitment to providing financial stability, recognition, and growth opportunities to this crucial segment of the Indian economy.
Beginning on July 1, 2023, a campaign was launched by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA), revising the targets to be achieved under the Scheme.

The "SVANidhi se Samriddhi" initiative, launched on January 4, 2021, aims to connect beneficiaries' families to eight Government of India socio-economic welfare schemes, promoting holistic development.
The scheme employs Aadhaar-based e-KYC, utilizes an end-to-end IT platform, and employs SMS-based notifications for application status updates.
All lending institutions, including NBFCs/MFIs and DPAs, have partnered with the aim to alleviate urban poverty in India.
Promoting digital transactions, participating Lending Institutions/Banks, and Digital Payment Aggregators (DPAs) have offered digital onboarding and training.

[On 18 December, 2020](https://youtu.be/dl_Vxo_H_yI) [[2]]() , Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched [Revised Scheme to Kisan Credit Card](https://rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/content/pdfs/CRB5100512AN.pdf) [[3]]() (KCC) which aims at providing adequate and timely credit support from the banking system under a single window to the farmers for their cultivation and other needs. **2\. Objectives/ Purpose** Kisan Credit Card (KCC) scheme meets the financial requirements of farmers at various stages of farming. [The scheme aims at providing adequate and timely credit support from the banking system under a single window](https://pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1515649) [[4]]() with flexible and simplified procedure to the farmers for their cultivation and other needs as indicated below: [To meet the short-term credit requirements for cultivation of crops](https://rbi.org.in/scripts/BS_ViewMasCirculardetails.aspx?id=11034) ; Post-harvest expenses; Produce marketing loan; Consumption requirements of farmer household; [Working capital for maintenance of farm assets and activities allied to agriculture;](https://www.iob.in/new-kisan-credit-card) [[5]]() Investment credit requirement for agriculture and allied activities.

Short-term loans and term loans are governed by different interest rates. At present, short term crop loans up to ₹ 3 lakh are covered under Interest Subvention Scheme/Prompt Repayment Incentive scheme of the Government of India. Further, repayment schedule and norms are different for short term and term loans. Hence, in order to have operational and accounting convenience, the card limit is to be bifurcated into separate sub-limits for short term cash credit limit cum savings account and term loans. Drawing limit for short term cash credit should be fixed based on the cropping pattern. The amount(s) for crop production, repair and maintenance of farm assets and consumption may be allowed to be drawn as per the convenience of the farmer. For term loans, installments may be allowed to be withdrawn based on the nature of investment and repayment schedule drawn as per the economic life of the proposed investments. **For Marginal Farmers** A flexible limit of ₹ 10,000 to ₹ 50,000 may be provided (as Flexi KCC) based on the land holding and crops grown including post-harvest warehouse storage related credit needs and other farm expenses, consumption needs, etc., plus small term loan investment(s) like purchase of farm equipment(s), establishing mini dairy/backyard poultry as per assessment of the Branch Manager without relating it to the value of land. The composite KCC limit is to be fixed for a period of five years on this basis. ( [Illustration II](https://rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/content/pdfs/04MCKCC03072017_AN2.pdf) ) **6\. Achievements** As part of the [Atmanirbhar Bharat Package](https://pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1665849) [[12]]() , the Government has announced to cover 2.5 crore farmers under the Kisan Credit Card (KCC) scheme with a credit boost of Rs. 2 lakh crores through a special saturation drive. As a result of concerted and sustained efforts by the banks and other stakeholders in the direction of providing access to concessional credit by the farmers, including Fishermen and Dairy farmers, a major milestone target of covering more than 1.5 crore farmers under KCC, with sanctioned credit limit of Rs.1.35 lakh crore has been achieved.

citations.title: Ama Krushi Transition Insights Report
excerpts: In 2018, with support from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF), PxD undertook the develop- ment of “Ama Krushi” - a customized, two-way digital information service to provide millions of smallholder farmers in Odisha with targeted, relevant and actionable advice.

Ama Krushi evolved from a 1 million farmer program providing Interactive Voice Response (IVR) based advice to rice farmers to include additional delivery channels (live call center, radio, in-person hybrid models), partnerships across new content areas (women’s groups, kitchen gardens, livestock, fisheries), and new features (collecting feedback about extension worker performance, schemes).

Ama Krushi was concep- tualized as a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) program, where PxD would build, iterate on, and scale this service to reach 1 million rice farmers over 3 years, following which implementation and funding would be handed over entirely to the government.

At the time of transition, the service was reaching over 3.2 million farmers and covered 28 value chains including several crops, animals and fisheries - a significant expansion from the original scope.

Importantly, the cost of adding an additional user to the service at scale is proving extremely low (< $0.22 per user per year as of 2023), making it extremely attractive for govern- ments to pay for implementation costs at scale.

The Ama Krushi service continues to run uninterrupted, and continues to scale – reaching over 5 million farmers as of June 2023. – and evolve – with new functionality including AI-driven chatbots continuing to be developed on top of the core service.

PxD completed the transfer of the Ama Krushi service to government ownership in June 2022, with day-to-day management support provided by Tatwa Technologies, a local firm contracted by the government through a public procurement process.

Overall, the transition was a success: the service is now entirely government-funded, and govern- ment-owned, with nominated officials from Department of Agriculture and Farmers Empowerment (DAFE) providing strategic oversight.
PxD also transferred its technology platform, ‘PADDY’, monitoring protocols, content databases and more under the BOT arrangement.
